draft.title: What superannuation is
card: Superannuation, or super, is money set aside during a person's working life. It is kept until retirement so they have an income when they stop work.
The money is held by a super fund. The fund invests it, for example in shares and property, so it can grow over time.
Super is preserved. This means people usually cannot take it out until they reach a set age and retire, not whenever they like.
Super is different from everyday savings. It is meant to pay for living costs in later life, not for short-term spending.
draft.remember: Super is saved and invested during work, then used for income in retirement.

a.q: What is the main purpose of superannuation?
opts: To give people an income after they stop working
To pay for a person's spending while they work
To let people buy a home as soon as they wish
To pay the tax a person owes each year
a.why: Super is saved during working life so there is money to live on in retirement. It is not meant for spending during work, because it is usually kept until a set age.
a.clue: Think about when the money is meant to be used.

b.q: Jarrah is 30 and has money in his super fund. He asks if he can withdraw it next month to take a holiday. What is the best answer?
opts: No, super is usually kept until he reaches retirement age
Yes, because the money in the fund is his to spend
Yes, as long as he tells the fund the reason first
No, because the fund has already spent the money
b.why: Super is preserved, so people usually cannot take it out until a set age and retirement. The money is not spent: the fund invests it so it can grow for his later life.
b.clue: Is super meant for short-term spending?

a.best: To give people an income after they stop working

b.best: No, super is usually kept until he reaches retirement age

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a qualifier ('usually'), which makes it stand out as the careful, hedged answer. A student could pick it without knowing the idea. Consider giving a distractor a similar hedge.
